baltit-fort.story: Welcome to Baltit Fort, a palatial fort in the Hunza Valley, near Karimabad in Gilgit-Baltistan, northern Pakistan. Its core structures — including the defensive stone and timber tower — date to the 8th century CE, and its architecture reflects Tibetan influences. In the 16th century, Ayasho II, the Mir of Hunza, married Shah Khatun, a princess from Skardu and granddaughter of Ali Sher Khan Anchan; her father-in-law Abdal Khan sent artisans who rebuilt the fort and also sent a cannon bearing the date 1539 CE. Abandoned by the Mirs of Hunza in 1945, the decaying fort was restored through a programme supported by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture and completed in 1996, and it is now a museum run by the Baltit Heritage Trust.
baltit-fort.name: Baltit Fort

altit-fort.story: In Altit town in the Hunza Valley in Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan, stands Altit Fort, once home to the hereditary rulers of the Hunza state who carried the title of 'Mir' before they moved to the nearby Baltit Fort. The fort, and especially the Shikari Tower, is around 1100 years old, making it the oldest monument in Gilgit-Baltistan, and it received the UNESCO Asia Pacific Heritage Award for Cultural Heritage Conservation in 2011. The area around the fort is inhabited by Burusho people, and the word 'Altit' means 'this side down' in Burushaski. After poor conditions, it was restored by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture with aid from the Government of Norway, and as a tourist site with small rooms and low portals with exquisite wood carvings, it has been open to the public since 2007.
altit-fort.name: Altit Fort

karimabad-hunza.story: Traveller, Karimabad—formerly Baltit—is the capital of the Hunza District in Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan, in the disputed Kashmir region, and it was named in honour of Karim Aga Khan, the late spiritual leader of the Shia Ismaili Nizari community. The town sits on the western bank of the Hunza River, opposite Nagar Valley in the lower Hunza Valley, at 8,200 feet, built on stone-walled and steep-sloping terraces. Historically, it was a caravan stop for travellers journeying through the Hindu Kush mountains en route to the Vale of Kashmir. Framed by deep gorges and snow-clad peaks such as Rakaposhi, Diran, Golden Peak, and Ultar Peak—each with dedicated viewpoints in and around town—Karimabad is reached primarily via a hill road from Aliabad.
karimabad-hunza.name: Karimabad

ganish.story: For a traveller, Ganish is a historic settlement on the banks of the Hunza river, dating back to around a 1,000 years. It is the oldest and first settlement on the ancient Silk Road in the Hunza Valley, where you can find ancient watchtowers, traditional mosques, religious centers, and a reservoir. This place has been a major town for travelers since the days of the Silk Road—now the Karakorum Highway runs right through it—and in 2003 it was awarded the UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award for Culture Heritage Conservation. As you look around, remember that the Nagar Valley is directly opposite Ganish and much of Hunza Valley, and the Altit Fort is 15 km to the north-east.
ganish.name: Ganish

attabad-lake.story: For a traveller, Attabad Lake, also known as Hunza Lake, offers boating, jet-skiing, fishing, and various winter sports, attracting attention year-round in the Gojal region of Gilgit-Baltistan. It was formed in January 2010 when a significant landslide impounded the water in the Hunza River in Attabad village. The Attabad landslide on 4 January 2010 occurred about 14 km east of Karimabad
attabad-lake.name: Attabad Lake

gulmit.story: For a traveller, Gulmit is a centuries-old historic town in upper Hunza, Gilgit Baltistan, Pakistan, with mountains, peaks and glaciers, and it is a tourist spot with historic places, hotels, and a museum. Before 1974, when Hunza was a princely state, Gulmit was the summer capital, and after the state was abolished it became the tehsil’s seat of government; its oldest intact house is more than six centuries old. In Gojal Valley, most people have Central Asian ancestry, speak Wakhi, and belong to the Shia Ismaili sect of Islam, while Ondra fort is the most prominent fort, perched on Ondra hill overlooking Gulmit and Ghulkin villages. It is believed that Qutlug Baig built Ondra fort in the 16th century and was the first Wakhi ruler to establish rule in Gulmit, after Su Malik and Mir Malik had stopped in Gulmit, liked it, and decided to live there.
gulmit.name: Gulmit

borith-lake.story: Traveller, you can find Borith Lake in Gojal, the Upper Hunza Valley in Gilgit–Baltistan, northern Pakistan, lying about 2,600 metres above sea level and just 2 km north of Hussaini village. You can reach this saline lake by a 2 km paved route from Husseini village, adjacent to Gulmit, or by a 2–3 hour trekking route directly from Gulmit across the end of the Ghulkin glacier. Here the site is a sanctuary for migrating wildfowl, and between March and June you can witness large numbers of ducks arriving from warmer parts of southern Pakistan to rest on their way northwards to the cooler waters of central Asia, while from September–November the migration occurs in reverse with the onset of winter. From the lake, a one-hour trek each way brings you to Hussaini Glacier, and a longer walk to Passu Gar Glacier crosses both Ghulkin Glacier and Borith Lake, with a path from Passu Glacier leading down to the Karakorum Highway.
borith-lake.name: Borith Lake

hussaini-suspension-bridge.story: If you travel from the Karakoram Highway, you can reach the Hussaini Suspension Bridge, a pedestrian hanging bridge over the Hunza River in Gilgit Baltistan’s Karakoram range. Originally built for local access, it has become a popular tourist attraction because of its striking structure and dramatic location, providing a passageway between the Hussaini and Zarabod villages of Upper Hunza in the Gojal area of Hunza District. Its 194 m suspended structure consists of rectangular wooden planks held by six main ropes, with larger spaces between consecutive planks intended to resist wobbly vibrations when driven by the wind. To visit and cross, follow the necessary precautions such as the use of life jackets.
hussaini-suspension-bridge.name: Hussaini Suspension Bridge

passu.story: Traveller, along the Karakoram Highway in the Gojal Valley of Upper Hunza, you will find Passu, a small village in Gilgit Baltistan, Northern Pakistan. It sits along the Hunza River, about 20 kilometres from Gulmit and about 147 kilometres upriver from Gilgit, near the tongue of the Passu Glacier and just south of the Batura Glacier, which is 56 kilometres long and the seventh-longest non-polar glacier in the world. From here, you can take in landscapes and views of the 7,478-metre Passu Sar, the Passu Glacier, the Batura Glacier, and Tupopdan—also called Passu Cones or Passu Cathedral—standing at 6,106 metres north of the village and known as the most photographed peak of the region. The village is predominantly inhabited by Wakhi people, who speak the Wakhi language and are homogeneously Ismaili, and who migrated in waves from Wakhan between 1870 and 1948 to different areas of northern Pakistan.
passu.name: Passu

passu-glacier.story: Traveller, beneath Passu Peak in the western Karakoram Range, Passu Glacier lies south of Passu village in Upper Hunza, also known as Gojal, in the Hunza District of Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan. Its meltwater supports local agriculture and nearby settlements, where communities developed a sophisticated irrigation system centuries ago to manage and distribute the water. At its front to the east lies Passu Lake, which drains into the Hunza River, and the glacier falls under the Northwest Karakoram climatic regime, with maximum precipitation in winter and occasional rainfall in spring and summer. During the British colonial era, explorers and surveyors documented their travels through the Karakoram, including Dr. Philips Christiaan Visser and Jenny Visser-Hooft, who surveyed about two-thirds of the glacier in 1925, and later Major W. R. F. Trevelyan and Captain M. H. Berkeley, who in May 1932 described it as “healthy,” with clean white ice extending to its snout.
passu-glacier.name: Passu Glacier

batura-glacier.story: Traveller, the Batura Glacier is 57 km long and is one of the largest and longest glaciers outside of the polar regions, lying in the upper Hunza (Gojal) region of Hunza District, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan, just north of the Batura and Passu massifs. It flows west to east, and its lower portions are a grey sea of rocks and gravelly moraine, bordered by a few summer villages and pastures with herds of sheep, goats, cows and yaks, where roses and juniper trees are common. Around it, the deep valleys are dry, with only about 10 cm of precipitation per year, while its upper reaches are coldest and its middle and lower parts more temperate. As of 1984, its terminus was about 0.5 km above the Karakoram Highway, and it has since retreated, with both backwasting and downwasting occurring.
batura-glacier.name: Batura Glacier

ultar-sar.story: As you travel the Karakoram Highway through the Hunza Valley, Ultar rises near Karimabad—the southeasternmost major peak of the Batura Muztagh in the Karakoram, about 10 km northeast of town. Though not among the highest Karakoram peaks, its south flank climbs over 5,300 metres above the Hunza River in only about 9 km, and with the river bending around it, it is a visually striking peak. In the 1990s it was famous as supposedly the world’s highest unclimbed independent peak, though that was incorrect because Gangkhar Puensum in Bhutan is higher and remains unclimbed and off-limits as of 2007. After fifteen expeditions made attempts in the 1980s and 1990s with no summits but a number of fatalities, the first two summits were made in 1996 by separate Japanese expeditions.
ultar-sar.name: Ultar
